title: The Gibbon’s Gaze: A Mirror Into the Human Mind - Nautilus
gist: Gibbons—the only group of 'lesser apes'—are among the least studied apes in cognitive research, and a new study argues they are essential to reconstructing the evolutionary origins of the human mind.

insights.claim: Gibbons form the single group of 'lesser apes' and receive far less scientific attention than the great apes, humanity's closest primate relatives.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Signals a research gap and a fresh subject area for comparative cognition studies.
insights.locator: It turns out there’s just one group, gibbons

insights.claim: Gibbons remain one of the least studied ape groups in cognitive research despite their evolutionary importance, according to Kyoto University primatologist Makiko Uchikoshi.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Flags an under-explored scientific niche where new findings could have outsized novelty.
insights.quote: Despite their evolutionary importance, gibbons remain one of the least studied ape groups in cognitive research.

insights.claim: Understanding the evolutionary origins of the human mind requires comparative cognitive studies spanning the entire ape lineage, not just the great apes.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Frames why gibbon cognition matters to broader questions about human evolution.
insights.quote: Understanding the evolutionary origins of the human mind requires comparative studies across the ape lineage.

insights.claim: A new study in the journal Animal Behavior and Cognition aims to raise the profile of gibbon cognition research.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Marks an emerging line of published work to track in primate cognition.
insights.locator: a new study published in the journal Animal Behavior and Cognition
